name: TigerGraph
license: Proprietary; Community Edition is free, including for production use within its limits
summary: A distributed graph database built for parallel traversals over very large graphs, queried with its own SQL-like language GSQL (and openCypher), self-managed or as the Savanna cloud service.
intro: TigerGraph calls its design a native parallel graph: each machine stores part of the graph and computes on it locally, and the parts coordinate by passing messages. The storage engine (GSE) and the processing engine (GPE) are written in C++, and a REST server, RESTPP, takes requests and manages tasks. Graphs are schema-first: you declare vertex and edge types, then run loading jobs. Queries are written in GSQL, a SQL-like, Turing-complete language designed in 2015, so whole algorithms can be written as queries. Most of openCypher is also accepted, embedded in GSQL, and TigerGraph says it supports ISO GQL too. Each GSQL query or REST call is one ACID transaction; isolation is read committed, implemented with MVCC, a write is complete only when every replica has applied it, and committed data goes to a write-ahead log on disk. The engine also stores vectors for hybrid graph and vector search.

Community Edition is free for production use on a single server, with up to 16 CPUs, 200 GB of graph data and 100 GB of vectors. Enterprise, priced through sales, adds clustering, high availability and disaster recovery, role-based access control and rolling upgrades. Savanna, the managed service that replaced TigerGraph Cloud Classic, keeps storage and compute separate so each scales on its own; workspaces are billed by the hour, from $1 for TG-00 (2 vCPUs, 16 GB of RAM) to $256 for TG-64 (512 vCPUs, 4 TB) in US regions, with a free trial. Data from a lakehouse is copied in: Iceberg tables through Kafka Connect or the Spark connector, Delta Lake and Hudi through Spark. A March 2026 paper by TigerGraph and Purdue researchers describes GraphLake, a research engine built on TigerGraph that queries Iceberg tables in place.
strengths: Scales out: the graph is partitioned across machines and queries run in parallel on each part
GSQL is Turing complete, so PageRank-style algorithms and multi-step analytics run inside the database, and openCypher and GQL are accepted too
A free Community Edition that allows production use, up to 16 CPUs and 200 GB of graph data
Savanna separates storage from compute and bills workspaces by the hour
limits: Closed source, and Enterprise pricing is not published
Schema-first: vertex and edge types must be declared before loading, and openCypher queries silently skip vertices that lack an attribute instead of returning NULL
Isolation is read committed, not serializable
Lakehouse data has to be loaded through Spark or Kafka Connect, which means a second copy and a pipeline to keep it fresh; the smallest Savanna workspace costs about $730 a month if left running

story: TigerGraph began in 2012 as GraphSQL, founded by Ruoming Jin, Li Chen, Mingxi Wu, Like Gao and Yu Xu. Its query language, GSQL, was designed in 2015 by Mingxi Wu and Alin Deutsch as a SQL-like but Turing-complete language for graph analytics.

The company came out of stealth in September 2017 under the name TigerGraph, with $33 million in funding, and raised $32 million in 2019 and a $105 million Series C in February 2021. It pitched a single system for transactions and analytics that could scale to hundreds of terabytes and trillions of edges, for uses such as fraud detection and customer 360.

Savanna, a rebuilt cloud service with storage and compute separated, entered beta on 29 April 2024. In March 2025 it announced a Community Edition that is free for production use on one server and includes vector search and Iceberg loading. In March 2026 researchers from TigerGraph and Purdue University published GraphLake, a design for running GSQL over Iceberg tables without loading them first.

choices.choice: Storage and computation on the same machines
choices.why: The native parallel graph keeps each partition of the graph next to the code that processes it and coordinates by message passing, so a traversal over billions of edges can run on many machines at once.

choices.choice: Its own language instead of only Cypher or Gremlin
choices.why: GSQL was designed to feel like SQL while being Turing complete, so analysts can write full graph algorithms as queries rather than calling external libraries.

choices.choice: Separate storage and compute in the cloud service
choices.why: Savanna lets storage and compute scale independently, so a workspace can be resized or stopped without moving the data.
